topic.title: Why One Eye Turns In or Out
topic.audience_question: Why can one eye turn inward or outward, how does this affect vision, and when is a new eye turn urgent?
topic.pubmed_query: strabismus esotropia exotropia amblyopia children adults sudden onset diplopia treatment

sources.title: Strabismus
sources.abstract: The American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus defines strabismus as eye misalignment, describes inward, outward, and vertical forms, explains amblyopia risk, and reviews optical, prism, exercise, and surgical treatments.
sources.journal: American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus

sources.title: Esotropia
sources.abstract: AAPOS explains that esotropia is inward turning of one or both eyes. Constant crossing at any age, or any crossing beyond about four months of age, should be assessed. Causes and treatment vary with onset, focusing error, constancy, and associated disease.
sources.journal: American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus

sources.title: Exotropia
sources.abstract: AAPOS describes exotropia as outward turning that may be intermittent or constant. Intermittent exotropia may become noticeable with fatigue, illness, bright light, or distance viewing and may become more frequent over time.
sources.journal: American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus

sources.title: Amblyopia
sources.abstract: AAPOS explains that amblyopia is reduced vision caused by abnormal visual development in childhood. Strabismus can lead the brain to ignore one eye, and early detection and treatment can prevent permanent vision loss.
sources.journal: American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus

sources.title: Adult Strabismus
sources.abstract: AAPOS explains that adult eye misalignment can cause double vision and impair depth perception and daily function. Prism and eye-muscle surgery may improve alignment and symptoms, and treatment is reconstructive rather than merely cosmetic.
sources.journal: American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus

sources.title: Screening, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Pediatric Ocular Diseases
sources.abstract: This peer reviewed clinical review describes childhood vision screening, strabismus and amblyopia detection, and current treatments. Early identification of visual disruption can prevent lifelong impairment.

sources.title: Signs and Symptoms of Stroke
sources.abstract: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists sudden trouble seeing, weakness or numbness, speech difficulty, loss of balance, and severe unexplained headache as stroke warning signs requiring immediate emergency action.
sources.journal: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

episode.title: E48: Why One Eye Turns In or Out
episode.hook: Hello and welcome to the Your Only Doc podcast. Imagine taking a family photograph and noticing that one child's eye points toward the nose while the other looks at the camera. Or imagine waking as an adult and suddenly seeing two images because one eye no longer lines up. Eye misalignment is called strabismus. It can be constant or intermittent, begin in childhood or adulthood, and mean very different things depending on when it starts.

sections.heading: The high yield summary
sections.narration: Too busy? Here is your high yield summary. An inward turn is esotropia, an outward turn is exotropia, and an eye can also sit higher or lower than the other. Children may suppress the image from one eye and develop amblyopia without complaining of double vision. Adults with a new eye turn often see double and need prompt assessment. Sudden misalignment with severe headache, weakness, numbness, speech trouble, imbalance, drooping eyelid, unequal pupils, or trauma is an emergency.

sections.heading: Alignment requires teamwork
sections.narration: Six muscles move each eye, but alignment depends on much more than muscle strength. The brain must coordinate both eyes so they point at the same target and combine two images into one. Strabismus may affect one eye or alternate between them. It may appear only when tired or focusing at a certain distance, or remain present all the time. The direction and pattern help identify the cause.

sections.heading: Inward and outward turns behave differently
sections.narration: Esotropia points an eye toward the nose. Some children cross because farsighted focusing also pulls the eyes inward, and proper glasses may greatly improve alignment. Exotropia points an eye outward. An intermittent outward drift may appear when a person is tired, ill, daydreaming, looking far away, or in bright sunlight. Neither pattern can be diagnosed reliably from one photograph, because camera angle and facial anatomy can create a false appearance.

sections.heading: When a baby's crossing needs assessment
sections.narration: Small intermittent crossing can occur during the first few months while visual control develops. Constant crossing at any age is concerning, and any inward turn that continues beyond about four months should be examined. A wide nasal bridge or eyelid folds can make straight eyes look crossed, called pseudostrabismus, but appearance alone cannot prove that the eyes are aligned. Pediatric eye examination settles the question.

sections.heading: Amblyopia is not the same as strabismus
sections.narration: Strabismus describes where the eyes point. Amblyopia describes reduced vision because the developing brain did not learn to use an eye normally. When a child's eyes point in different directions, the brain may ignore one image to avoid confusion. The child may never report blur because the stronger eye takes over. Glasses, patching, or atropine may treat amblyopia, but eye alignment may need separate treatment. Earlier care gives visual development the best chance.

sections.heading: A new adult eye turn needs an explanation
sections.narration: Adults may have childhood strabismus that returns, but a new turn can result from a cranial nerve palsy, thyroid eye disease, trauma, diabetes-related nerve injury, myasthenia, orbital disease, or stroke. New double vision is common because an adult brain usually does not suppress the second image. Covering either eye may stop binocular double vision temporarily, but this does not identify the cause and should not delay assessment.
on_screen: New misalignment often causes double vision
Temporary covering is not a diagnosis

sections.heading: Know the emergency combinations
sections.narration: Call emergency services for sudden eye misalignment or double vision with weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, confusion, severe unexplained headache, trouble walking, dizziness, or loss of balance. Sudden drooping eyelid, unequal pupils, severe eye or head pain, or recent head and orbital trauma also need emergency evaluation. Even if the symptoms disappear after minutes, a transient ischemic attack remains possible and still requires urgent medical care.
on_screen: Sudden double vision can be neurological
Check pupils, eyelids, speech, and balance

sections.heading: How clinicians measure and treat it
sections.narration: Now, let us go deeper. Examination measures alignment at distance and near, with each eye covered in turn and in different gaze positions. Clinicians test vision in each eye, focusing power, eye movement, pupils, depth perception, and eye health. Treatment follows the pattern and goal. Options include glasses, amblyopia therapy, prisms, selected exercises, botulinum toxin, or eye-muscle surgery. Adult surgery can improve function and quality of life; it is not merely cosmetic.
on_screen: Match treatment to the cause and goal

sections.heading: Three essential takeaways
sections.narration: Number one, strabismus means eye misalignment, while amblyopia means reduced visual development, and a child can have either or both. Number two, constant crossing at any age, crossing beyond early infancy, or an increasingly frequent outward drift deserves a complete eye examination. Number three, seek emergency care for sudden eye turning or double vision with headache, weakness, numbness, speech change, imbalance, eyelid droop, unequal pupils, severe pain, or trauma.

episode.closing: On the next episode, we will explain why your eyes can struggle to work together up close, including convergence insufficiency, reading symptoms, useful tests, and treatments. Until then, remember that straight-looking eyes do not guarantee equal vision, and a new eye turn should never be dismissed.
episode.description: Strabismus can turn one eye inward, outward, upward, or downward. This episode explains esotropia, exotropia, amblyopia risk, childhood and adult patterns, examination, treatment, and emergency warning signs.
